newsitem.title: PERU: Peru gov't, rebels to resume crisis talks - reports.
newsitem.headline: Peru gov't, rebels to resume crisis talks - reports.

text.p: Peru's government and Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages were poised to restart face-to-face talks on Monday after negotiations to end the 83-day crisis were abruptly called off last week, local news reports said.
Peruvian newspapers and radio said mediators and rebels at a 2 1/2-hour meeting on Sunday set the stage for talks to resume between the government and Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).

The reports, citing members of a three-man mediating panel, said government negotiator Domingo Palermo and MRTA chief Nestor Cerpa would meet on Monday for the first time since last week, when rebels abruptly called off direct talks.
No starting time was given for the renewed talks.

Two panel members, who met with rebels to try to kick-start direct talks with the government, told reporters on Sunday that discussions with the MRTA would resume on Monday but it was not clear if the talks involved the government.
"Our message today is that the discussions will continue tomorrow. In the next week, the discussions should be important ones," Canadian envoy Anthony Vincent, a mediator, said.
"We ask everyone involved to let these conversations continue in the way they have, seeking a solution that, although difficult, is viable," added Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, another panel member.
Nine rounds of talks between the MRTA and the government had brought some progress toward a bloodless end to the crisis, with both sides on Wednesday swapping formal proposals for the first time.
But a day later, the MRTA suspended a 10th meeting aimed at reaching a solution to the nearly 12-week siege, alleging security forces planned to attack the residence through a tunnel.
President Alberto Fujimori has dodged questions about the tunnel and officials, including Defence Minister Tomas Castillo Meza, deny its existence.
But security force sources confirmed four tunnels were dug in recent weeks while police blared music from loudspeakers and local papers published details, including maps, of the tunnels.

Rebels stormed the residence on Dec. 17 and took hundreds of VIPs hostage. Most were released in the first weeks of the siege but the MRTA has kept its most prized bargaining chips, including Fujimori's brother Pedro, the Japanese and Bolivian envoys and dozens of Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
